Atlassian publishes the Jira Cloud platform REST API as a machine-readable OpenAPI 3.0.1 document (info title "The Jira Cloud platform REST API", 433 paths), linked from the REST v3 reference intro, alongside a vendor-generated Postman collection export.

The REST API is explicitly versioned: "This documentation is for version 3 of the Jira Cloud platform REST API, which is the latest version. Version 2 and version 3 of the API offer the same collection of operations" (v3 adds Atlassian Document Format support). The reference itself is a static SSR reference; its runnable affordance is the generated Postman collection, not an in-page console.

Atlassian documents product sandboxes: "A sandbox is an isolated environment where you can experiment and test changes safely before applying them in production. Every sandbox works like a replica of your production environment", available for Jira (and Confluence, JSM, JPD) on Premium or Enterprise plans. The page notes a sandbox "is not a production environment" and is not covered by the SLA.

For developers, Atlassian provisions free development instances: "Forge can provision a demo development site when you need an Atlassian site for developing and testing an app" ("Demo sites are active for 90 days by default"), and the getting-started docs point to creating a traditional Atlassian cloud developer site. (The cloud-development-environment page itself sits behind an id.atlassian.com login; these reachable pages document the surface.)

Atlassian publishes a formal REST API policy with a deprecation commitment: a deprecated REST API in the cloud environment must remain available in its original form "for at least 6 months" (with exceptions for critical security, reliability, or data-integrity fixes), deprecated endpoints should return RFC 9745 response headers, and a dedicated API-versioning section describes how versions are exposed.

Jira has always been very quick and responsive for me. It offers a good amount of customization too... Never once encountered a major bug in it either.
Biggest problem when I used it, could not assign anything to more than 1 person.
Jira is heavy and slow - its model of limited transitions is fundamentally flawed, encouraging micromanagement and making mistakes hard to undo.
I personally find Jira miles more confusing than Radar after having used both extensively.
I routinely lose data in jira, like saving errors. Dragging and dropping attachments sometimes causes the page to crash and reload. Everything in the UI moves around or obscured behind some tabs.
Also it's really annoying when I try to copy something from a ticket description but it starts editing the whole description field.
As a developer, once I finish my ticket I assign it to a QA. Then I can never get back to the ticket... completed tickets aren't assigned to me, they're assigned to QA.

Single letter hotkeys are pretty bad. If it's not an input field you've focused but the page itself, you might assign the ticket to yourself and set it to some crazy state before you realize the focus is all wrong.
Jira is bloated. Full stop. It feels like there isn't a strong unified product vision for Jira. It's just trying to solve everything.

Why do I need to mark an epic as closed two different ways? Why is it really difficult to see what tickets were in a closed sprint? Why is it so slow or why does it sometimes get in infinite reload loop? Features randomly break like the ability to create tickets from confluence.
Due to the slow loading, I ended up writing some simple Jira API wrapper scripts for submitting bug reports quicker in our systems.
Trying to do something as seemingly simple as create a useful saved search in JIRA is so painful I can't imagine its creation was not an act of sabotage.
Once a JIRA shop, we moved everything to Asana years ago, after trying literally everything else. Our design team just could not get on board with JIRA. It was too much 'work' to track their efforts.
If you know the tool well, and your company doesn't have stupid technical workflows and human processes, it's just great.
Please, kill Jira and Confluence. I hate Atlassian tools so much. The user interfaces are sluggish no matter the hardware you're using... it's a shame it became almost a standard in our industry.
One of the things I like most about Jira is the ability to execute useful queries via REST on the data stored in there.
Does Plane offer an alternative for JQL (Jira Query Language)? That's what I appreciate most about Jira.

Having used both extensively, a former Apple user found Jira 'miles more confusing' than Apple's Radar. Radar's native table view allowed multi-select and drag and drop, though the underlying design paradigm was the same.

Jira can be a good issue tracker if properly configured, but using it for top-down, high-level planning has always been frustrating. Advice: ignore the portfolio add-ons, plan down to the epic level in something like Excel, then map that to Jira tickets.
Jira is heavy and slow. Its model of limited transitions encourages micromanagement and makes mistakes hard to undo. A lightweight kanban board like Trello worked better for this user.

Jira has always been quick and responsive for me, with good customization. Our custom workflow fits how we develop software. It has never limited what my teams wanted to do, and I've never hit a major bug in it.
Jira doesn't track dependencies very well. It is so flexible that many shops configure it to be nearly unusable, while others create workflows that work very well.

Jira helps workers see the big picture better than other tools in its class. Any issue can link to any other issue across projects and teams, such as linking bugs to the customer support issues that describe them. On-prem instances that are under-resourced or keep Lucene indexes on networked storage perform badly.
Jira is an incredibly flexible, unopinionated business process tool that suits software processes in larger organisations. Despite the criticism, this user has yet to see a better tool of its kind.
The biggest problem when I used it: you could not assign anything to more than one person.

The UI moves around a lot, so I'm anxious to click anything until all the loading spinners stop. Trying to copy text from a description starts editing the field. Once I assign a finished ticket to QA, there's no easy way to find all the tickets I've completed.
Jira needs dedicated admins, but companies adopt it without enough support. Every team configures things its own way until it grows into an unusable forest that can't be brought back to order.
Single-letter hotkeys are bad. If the page rather than an input field has focus, you can accidentally assign the ticket to yourself and set it to some crazy state before realizing it.

Coming from Apple's Radar, this user called Jira the worst. They routinely lose data to saving errors, and drag-and-drop attachments sometimes crash and reload the page. Workflows are too complicated, and the flexibility adds administrative hell.

Once a Jira shop, we moved everything to Asana after trying everything else. Our design team couldn't get on board with Jira; tracking their work was too much 'work'. Asana balances developer depth with high-level task management for other teams.

It's slow and navigation sucks, but with lean workflows it's 'good enough'. This user asks which competitor offers a visual workflow editor, custom statuses and transitions with conditions, custom screens and fields, time tracking, and permission schemes.

Why mark an epic closed two different ways? Why is it hard to see which tickets were in a closed sprint? It's slow, sometimes gets stuck in infinite reload loops, and features like creating tickets from Confluence randomly break.
A former part-time Jira admin chose Jira again at a new company and said they missed it. If you know the tool well and avoid stupid workflows, it's great; many people suffer from using it wrong.
Repeatedly hit walls trying to do basic things in JIRA. Creating a useful saved search is so painful it seems like an act of sabotage.
Workaround: because of slow loading, this user wrote simple Jira API wrapper scripts to submit bug reports more quickly.
I hate Atlassian tools. Jira's and Confluence's interfaces are sluggish no matter what hardware you use, and it's a shame they became almost an industry standard.
One of the things I like most about Jira is the ability to run useful queries via its REST API on the stored data. Jira alternatives usually ignore this.
